meta.name: How to Help a Dog With Arthritis at Home: A Room-by-Room Setup
meta.title_tag: How to Help a Dog With Arthritis at Home: Room by Room
meta.excerpt: The home changes vets recommend most are simple: better traction, easier access to beds, stairs and the car, short, regular walks and a leaner body weight, which has the strongest evidence. Here's how to set up each room for a dog with arthritis, plus what to track and bring to your vet.
meta.meta_description: A room-by-room home setup for a dog with arthritis: floors, beds, stairs, bowls and the car, plus weight, exercise and pain signs to review with your vet.
meta.author: Kailun Zhang

hero.alt: Older Golden Retriever walking on a non-slip runner over a hardwood floor — simple home changes that help dogs with arthritis

body_html:
Quick Answer: Start with grip and access: secured rugs on slick floors, short nails, a gate or ramp for stairs, and a padded, low-entry bed in a warm, dry spot. Keep your dog lean and walk little and often; in one small study, obese dogs with arthritis limped less after losing about 6% of body weight (Marshall et al., 2010). Never give human pain relievers such as ibuprofen, naproxen or acetaminophen (FDA). Ask your vet for a pain plan instead. Why ↓

Signs of Arthritis Owners Often Miss

Arthritis (osteoarthritis) rarely starts with an obvious limp. The Merck Veterinary Manual lists the usual signs as slowness to rise after rest, getting up front end first (or back end first), trouble with stairs, and less jumping and play; lameness can be subtle even in advanced disease. Other signs are easy to blame on age:

  • Sitting with a leg stuck out or rolled onto one hip, or "bunny hopping" (ACVS)
  • Hesitating before jumping onto the couch or into the car (ACVS, AVMA)
  • Sleeping more, playing less, or not wanting to be petted (AVMA)
  • Irritability and muscle loss (Cornell)

It isn't only an old-dog problem. In a North Carolina State study of 123 dogs aged 8 months to 4 years, 39.8% had arthritis on X-rays; owners had noticed signs in only about 30% of those whose arthritis was also painful, and just 2 of those dogs were treated (Enomoto et al., 2024; three authors disclosed Elanco ties). In UK clinic records, arthritis was diagnosed more often in Labradors, Golden Retrievers, heavier dogs and dogs over 8 (Anderson et al., 2018). Merck also lists German Shepherds among breeds prone to elbow problems that lead to arthritis.

Get a diagnosis first. Limping can also mean an injury, a nerve problem or cancer (VCA), so have your vet examine your dog before assuming it's arthritis, and promptly if the limp is sudden.

Bring evidence to your vet. Pain often hides in the exam room, so AAHA recommends videos of your dog rising and walking at home. Free, validated owner questionnaires such as the 11-question Canine Brief Pain Inventory (Penn Vet; Brown et al., 2008) and the 23-question LOAD (Walton et al., 2013) help track change (AAHA 2022). Mention restless nights too; they can signal pain as well as dog dementia.

Never Give Your Dog Human Pain Relievers

Ibuprofen, naproxen and aspirin are human NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), and in dogs they may last longer, be absorbed faster and reach higher blood levels (FDA). Acetaminophen can damage a dog's liver and red blood cells; vets occasionally use it under supervision, but never give it on your own. Don't use pills left over from another pet either. No over-the-counter NSAID for dogs is FDA-approved. If your dog has swallowed human pain pills, contact your vet, an emergency vet or an animal poison control center right away.

Which Changes Have Evidence Behind Them?

ChangeWhat the evidence shows
Keeping your dog leanStrongest: a lifetime study and a small weight-loss trial
Short, regular walksLimited but positive; in AAHA's top tier
Non-slip floors, ramps, padded bedsVet-recommended; untested in trials, low risk
WarmthVCA guidance; untested in trials
Raised bowlsConflicting; linked to bloat in large and giant breeds
Omega-3 fatty acidsThe best-supported supplement
Glucosamine and chondroitinMixed; a 2022 meta-analysis found no pain benefit

Floors: Stop the Slipping

Turning, rising and sitting all need grip. What vets suggest:

  • Runners and rugs with non-skid backing along your dog's daily routes, secured so they can't slide (AAHA 2023, VCA).
  • Yoga mats or interlocking foam tiles for larger areas (VCA, AAHA 2023).
  • Grip at the top and bottom of stairs and beside couches and beds (PetMD).
  • Short nails for better traction (VCA).
  • Toe grips, boots or socks for dogs that tolerate them (AAHA 2023, VCA).
  • Baby gates to keep your dog out of slick rooms you can't cover (VCA).

Beds, Resting Spots and Warmth

VCA suggests an orthopedic or memory-foam bed; AAHA asks for bedding that's "adequately padded." We found no study comparing bed types, so choose for comfort and access: an edge low enough to step over, with grip around it (PetMD). Dogs in pain often prefer quiet, protected spots (AAHA 2022), so put beds in the rooms your dog uses, somewhere that doesn't require stairs (AVMA, AAHA 2023).

VCA says cold, damp conditions may worsen stiffness and generally advises against outdoor living for dogs with arthritis. Merck lists warm compresses on sore joints; ask your vet how to use heat safely.

Stairs, Furniture and the Car

  • Stairs. Gate them when no one is around to supervise (VCA, PetMD).
  • Couches and beds. Ramps or pet steps keep favorite spots within reach without the jump (AAHA 2022, Cornell, AVMA).
  • The car. Many arthritic dogs start avoiding the jump (ACVS, AVMA). A car ramp helps, and VCA says most dogs learn ramps quickly. For big dogs, AAHA suggests a fitted, padded harness to help you lift.

Food Bowls: Should You Raise Them?

VCA suggests bowls between elbow and shoulder height to ease neck and back strain, and the AVMA and AAHA list raised feeding among home changes, but no study has tested whether raised bowls help arthritis.

In a study of 1,637 large and giant-breed dogs, about 20% of bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus) cases in large breeds and 52% in giant breeds were attributed to a raised bowl (Glickman et al., 2000). A 2017 evidence review found only two studies, with conflicting results, and advised floor feeding for at-risk dogs (Buckley, 2017).

So the evidence is mixed. With a Great Dane, Irish Wolfhound or other large, deep-chested dog, ask your vet first. For any dog, a non-skid mat under the bowls adds grip.

Weight: The Change With the Strongest Evidence

ACVS calls a slender body weight "by far the most critical aspect" of arthritis management; extra weight loads the joints, and fat releases inflammatory substances (Cornell).

In a Purina lifetime study of 48 Labrador Retrievers, one dog in each pair ate 25% less than its partner from 8 weeks old. The lean dogs lived longer (median 13.0 vs 11.2 years; Kealy et al., 2002) and first showed hip arthritis on X-rays at a median age of 12 instead of 6 (Smith et al., 2006). It's industry-funded and covers one breed, but AAHA says long-term studies strongly support keeping dogs lean.

Weight loss also helps dogs that already have arthritis. In 14 obese dogs, lameness improved from about 6% weight loss onward (Marshall et al., 2010); for a 70-pound dog, that's a little over 4 pounds. Ask your vet for a target weight and plan, with regular weigh-ins (VCA), and swap some treats for plain green beans or cucumber.

Exercise: Little and Often

ACVS recommends swapping running and jumping for leash walks and low-impact, consistent exercise that builds supporting muscle. Evidence in dogs is limited (AAHA 2022), but in 60 Labradors with hip dysplasia, longer daily exercise was linked to less lameness (Greene et al., 2013).

  • Short and regular. PetMD suggests starting with walks of up to 10–15 minutes, three or four times a day.
  • Softer options. Soft surfaces (Merck) and swimming (Cornell).

Ask your vet how far your dog should go (VCA).

Treatment Is Your Vet's Call

AAHA's 2022 pain guidelines (supported by grants from Zoetis, Elanco and other companies) rank two drug types as first-line for dogs, alongside omega-3s, weight control, exercise and home changes:

  • Prescription NSAIDs for dogs. Ask for the Client Information Sheet and expect blood tests before and during long-term use. Stop and call your vet if you see vomiting, diarrhea, black or bloody stool, poor appetite, less activity, or yellow gums or eyes. Never combine two NSAIDs, or an NSAID and a steroid (FDA).
  • Anti-NGF antibody injections. Bedinvetmab (Librela), FDA-approved in 2023 (FDA), is a monthly injection that blocks nerve growth factor, a driver of arthritis pain (Cornell). In the maker's US trial, 47.4% of treated dogs vs 36.6% on placebo met the day-28 success target (Michels et al., 2023). In December 2024 the FDA told vets about reported adverse events including wobbliness, seizures, weakness, incontinence, and increased thirst and urination, with death (including euthanasia) reported in some cases; an early-2025 label update added a client information sheet (dvm360). Some specialists report rapidly progressive joint damage (Farrell et al., 2025; von Pfeil et al., 2026), and a Zoetis-authored commentary disputes the 2025 analysis. In May 2026 EU regulators backed listing joint swelling, joint pain and arthritis as very rare side effects (EMA). Report new joint swelling or pain after an injection, and weigh benefits and risks with your vet.

AAHA ranks rehabilitation lower, as an add-on: range-of-motion work, therapeutic exercise and hydrotherapy can help mobility, but evidence for acupuncture and laser therapy is lacking (ACVS). Surgery can address some underlying causes (Cornell, ACVS).

Joint Supplements: What the Evidence Says

Omega-3s (EPA and DHA, mainly from fish oil) have the best evidence. AAHA ranks them first-line, and a 2022 meta-analysis found clear pain relief from omega-3 diets and supplements (Barbeau-Grégoire et al.). Omega-3s may not suit dogs with digestive or bleeding disorders (Tufts), and fish oil is high in calories, so for overweight dogs Cornell puts weight loss first. Plain cooked salmon is food, not a measured dose; let your vet pick any supplement and amount.

Glucosamine and chondroitin divide the sources. The same meta-analysis found a "very marked non-effect" and advised against recommending them for arthritis pain, and AAHA finds no evidence that non-omega-3 supplements relieve pain. Cornell specialists still think they may help slow progression. Supplements aren't regulated like drugs, so Cornell suggests a vet-recommended brand or one with the National Animal Supplement Council (NASC) seal.

Tell your vet everything you give. AAHA warns that turmeric has caused gut ulcers in humans and mice. Evidence for CBD is mixed (AAHA 2022), and the FDA hasn't approved cannabis products, including CBD, for any use in animals.

Room-by-Room Checklist

  • Hallways and living room: Secured runners, a padded bed near the family, a ramp to the couch.
  • Bedroom: A low-entry padded bed that doesn't require stairs.
  • Stairs: A gate for unsupervised times; grip at the top and bottom.
  • Kitchen: A mat under the bowls; ask your vet before raising them for a big dog.
  • Car: A ramp, plus a padded lifting harness for big dogs.
  • Yard and walks: Short leash walks on soft ground, then a warm, dry rest indoors.
  • Every month: A weigh-in, a nail check and a short video of your dog rising and walking. Seniors need vet checkups twice a year or more (AVMA); see when a dog becomes a senior.

Written by Kailun Zhang, who is not a veterinarian. This guide summarizes the veterinary sources listed below and isn't a substitute for advice from your vet.

Frequently Asked Questions

What can I give my dog for arthritis pain at home?

Nothing from your own medicine cabinet. Ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin and acetaminophen can seriously harm dogs, and no over-the-counter NSAID is FDA-approved for them (FDA). Home changes help, and your vet can prescribe pain relief made for dogs.

Is walking good for a dog with arthritis?

Usually, yes. Controlled, low-impact exercise helps most dogs with arthritis (VCA, ACVS), and longer daily exercise was linked to less lameness in Labradors with hip dysplasia (Greene et al., 2013). Keep walks short and frequent, and ask your vet how far to go.

Should I raise my arthritic dog's food bowl?

Maybe. VCA suggests elbow-to-shoulder height for comfort, but no study shows raised bowls help arthritis, and a large study linked them to bloat in large and giant breeds (Glickman et al., 2000). For large or deep-chested dogs, ask your vet first.

Do glucosamine supplements work for dogs?

Mixed at best. A 2022 meta-analysis found no pain benefit from glucosamine and chondroitin, though some Cornell specialists think they may help slow progression. Omega-3 fatty acids have stronger evidence (AAHA 2022). Ask your vet before starting any supplement.

Does cold weather make dog arthritis worse?

It may. VCA says cold, damp conditions may worsen stiffness and advises keeping dogs with arthritis warm, dry and indoors, though this hasn't been tested in trials. Dry your dog after wet walks (AAHA 2023) and keep beds out of drafts.

How do I know if my dog's arthritis is getting worse?

Watch for slower rising, more trouble with stairs or the car, less play, and more sleeping or irritability (Merck, AVMA, Cornell). Monthly videos and the Canine Brief Pain Inventory make changes easier to spot (AAHA 2022). Tell your vet rather than waiting for the next checkup.
